Commentary of Ibn Juzayy (al-Tashil) on surah 95, verses 1–3:

﴿By the fig and the olive﴾. On this there are two opinions. The first is that they are the fig that is eaten and the olive that is pressed for oil; God swore by them because of their excellence over the rest of the fruits. It is narrated that the Messenger of God (ﷺ) ate figs with his companions and said: "If I were to say that a fruit had come down from Paradise, I would say it is this, for the fruit of Paradise has no pits. So eat it, for it cuts off hemorrhoids and benefits gout." He (ﷺ) also said: "The olive is an excellent siwak; it is from the blessed tree, and it is my siwak and the siwak of the prophets before me."

The second opinion is that they are two places, and then it is disputed what they are. It is said they are two mountains in the Levant (al-Sham): one of them at Damascus, where figs grow, and the other at Iliya, where olives grow. So it is as if He said: "and the places where the fig and the olive grow." It is also said that the fig is the Mosque of Damascus and the olive is the Mosque of Jerusalem (Bayt al-Maqdis). It is said that the fig is the Mosque of Noah and the olive is the Mosque of Abraham. The more apparent view is that they are the two places in the Levant in which the birth and dwelling of Jesus took place. That is because God, after this, mentioned the Mount (Tur) on which He spoke to Moses and the city from which Muhammad (ﷺ) was sent. So the verse resembles what is in the Torah: "God came from Mount Sinai, rose up from Seir, which is the place of Jesus, and shone forth from the mountains of Paran," and Paran is Makkah. God swore by these places mentioned in the Torah because of their honor through the prophets mentioned.

﴿And Mount Sinin﴾. This is the mountain on which God spoke to Moses, and it is in the Levant. God attributed it to Sinin, and the meaning of Sinin is "blessed," so it is an idafa of the described to the describer (i.e., an adjective-like construction). It is also said that its meaning is "possessing trees," its singular being sinah; this is the view of al-Akhfash. Al-Zamakhshari said: "It is permissible that it be inflected like the sound masculine plural with waw and ya, and that the ya be obligatory with the nun moved by the inflectional vowels." (Here the Arabic word discussed is سينين, Sinin, inflected as a sound masculine plural with the ya and nun, its nun taking the case vowels.)

﴿And this secure city﴾. It is Makkah by agreement. Al-Amin is from amanah (trustworthiness) or from amn (security), due to His saying: ﴿Make this a secure city﴾ [al-Baqarah: 126].

﴿Indeed, We created man in the best of stature﴾. Regarding this there are two opinions. The first is that "the best of stature" means beauty of form, perfection of intellect, youth, and strength, while "the lowest of the low" means weakness, decrepitude, and senility. This is like His saying, ﴿And whomever We cause to grow old, We reverse him in creation﴾ [Yasin: 68], and His saying, ﴿Then made after strength weakness and gray hair﴾ [al-Rum: 54]. According to this opinion, His saying ﴿except those who believe﴾ is not connected to what precedes it, and the exception on this view is disjunctive (istithna' munqati', an exception not of the same category), meaning "but," because it falls outside the meaning of the preceding statement. The second opinion is that "the best of stature" is the natural disposition (fitrah) upon faith, and "the lowest of the low" is disbelief, or the disfiguring of the form in the Fire. On this view the exception is connected (istithna' muttasil, an exception of the same category), because those who believe and do righteous deeds will not be returned to the lowest of the low.

﴿Unfailing﴾ has already been mentioned.

﴿So what, after this, causes you to deny the Judgement?﴾ Regarding this there are two opinions. The first is that it is addressed to the Prophet ﷺ, and "the Judgement" (al-din) is his law. The meaning is: what thing makes the Judgement deny you after these signs that testify to the truth of your prophethood? The second is that it is addressed to the disbelieving human being, and "the Judgement" on this view means the law or the otherworldly recompense. The meaning of "causes you to deny" on this view is "makes you a liar," because whoever denies is a liar. The meaning is: what makes you a liar through your disbelief in the Judgement, after you have known that Allah created you in the best of stature and then returned you to the lowest of the low? Without doubt He is able to resurrect you as He was able to create you in this way. So why do you deny the resurrection and the recompense? Without doubt He is able to resurrect you as He was able to create you in this way. So why do you deny the resurrection and the recompense?
